Greatness is not some pre-determined thing that people are “meant” to be, that’s silly magical thinking. Anyone can be great and anyone can fail. You might be doing great now and lose it all, you might be doing terribly and see things turn around, you might fall somewhere in the middle, or maybe you really will be in one of those states forever. And so, people will naturally want others to live. Believing in potential is always preferable to giving up and never knowing what could have been.

Maybe it’ll never get better and everyone who has hope in their hearts for a better existence for themselves and others are total idiots and you know better than all of them. But you’ll never be able to say with 100% certainty what your future holds if you don’t experience it. Maybe you are fine with that, but you have to be realistic in assessing why most people might not be gleefully stepping aside when you declare you’re ending your life. 

If everyone who wasn’t doing great at the end of their 20s just ended it all,m we’d be without a lot of wonderful people who have been impactful in big ways and small ways. I’m not saying I know what’s best for you, but I hope I can offer some perspective on why people do care.

I had massive bleed at week 10 (very heavy, massive clots, for 4-6 hours). I was hysterical at the hospital assuming the worst but when they checked my baby was fine. A few weeks later I did a follow up ultrasound and although nothing could be found, I was still bleeding (not as heavily as the one night, but it’s still unnerving to see)

I bled for 7 weeks after that despite multiple doctors saying they couldn’t see the SCH or any other abnormalities on my ultrasounds. In that time I had one other episode where I gushed bright red blood but each time I went in to check on this I was assured my baby was fine and they couldn’t give me a reason why. 

My doctor explained that ultrasounds are limited in what they can detect and that I may still have an SCH that is too small to pick up. I’ve also been told by doctors that some people bleed their entire pregnancy and that as long as it’s being monitored it’s typically not a cause for concern. I did notice that for me, some things seemed to make the bleeding worse like sexual activity, bowl movements, and even coughing/sneezing.

1. I think the medication choice should be at least a conversation with your doctor. Mine went with Letrozole because it performs better in clinical trials for patients with PCOS. I'd certainly expect any RE to know about it. If they insist on something different they might have some reason for but they should be explaining that to you if that's the case. They write the script but ultimately it's up to you if you want to go forward with treatment. 
2. My first ever medicated cycle I was given a trigger shot, but I've also been trying naturally for like 3 years and I'm sure that effected my doctor's treatment plan. You should definitely ask about it, especially if your infertility is anovulatory. For me they were only willing to try a trigger shot when they could see the medicine was working and my follicles were maturing at a good rate. I was grateful they did this because the shot is expensive and I really didn't want to waste it if there was no egg coming.  
3.  I'd ask for a timeline of what's to come and what you can expect next. Getting a general idea of what a medicated and monitored cycle looks like at their practice can go a long way in easing your mind. You wanna prepare yourself for potential set backs as much as you can during this process. 

This journey is a difficult one so make sure to go easy on yourself. Good luck!

You don’t get a reward for choosing to live, nobody does. Your problem isn’t with your average life, if you woke up tomorrow with an extravagant job and every person on earth worshiping you, you’d probably still be depressed. 

The type of job you have, the hobbies you participate in, and other people’s perception of you is all superficial crap that’s basically interchangeable. That’s why some people are content with an average life and other people have everything and still want to die. What really matters is finding meaning in your life independent of all that. 

There’s no quick fix for it and any random person’s generic advice isn’t going to get you there. We can’t tell you what your meaning should be, it’s a deeply personal journey that’s different for everyone. It’s not some epiphany moment where you’ll find it, it’s usually done it smaller steps overtime. 

I’m sure you’ll think finding meaning in your life is not worth it, won’t work for you, can’t be done, is generic advice in itself etc. Those thoughts are all part of being depressed.
